14: # Skill Asset File Templates - Creation Guidelines
15: 
16: Templates and guidelines for creating asset files in AI agent skills.
17: 
18: ## 1. OVERVIEW
19: 
20: ### Location & Naming
21: 
22: **Location:** `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/assets/`
23: 
24: **Naming Convention:** kebab-case with the appropriate extension
25: 
26: | ✅ Valid Names | ❌ Invalid Names |
27: |---------------|-----------------|
28: | `frontmatter-templates.md` | `FrontmatterTemplates.md` (PascalCase) |
29: | `config-examples.yaml` | `config_examples.yaml` (snake_case) |
30: | `validation-checklist.md` | `ValidationChecklist.MD` (wrong case) |
31: | `emoji-reference.md` | `emojiReference.md` (camelCase) |
32: 
33: ### When to Create Assets
34: 
35: **Create an asset file when:**
36: - Templates users apply repeatedly
37: - Reference data >50 lines and self-contained
38: - Multiple examples of same pattern exist
39: - Lookup tables or decision matrices needed
40: - Template variations for different scenarios
41: 
42: **Keep in SKILL.md when:**
43: - Content <30 lines
44: - Tightly coupled to workflow logic
45: - Needs to be visible immediately (not progressive disclosure)
46: - Part of core instructions (RULES, WORKFLOW sections)
47: 
48: ---
49: 
50: ## 2. ASSET FILE TYPES
51: 
52: ### Template Files
53: **Purpose**: Provide copy-paste starting points for common tasks
54: 
55: **Naming**: `[content-type]-templates.md`
56: - Example: `frontmatter-templates.md`, `structure-templates.md`
57: 
58: **Structure**:
59: - One template per section
60: - Include field descriptions
61: - Show complete examples
62: - Explain when to use each template
63: 
64: **Use cases**:
65: - Document templates (SKILL.md, commands, knowledge files)
66: - Configuration templates (YAML, JSON)
67: - Code templates (functions, classes, modules)
68: 
69: ### Reference Files
70: **Purpose**: Provide lookup tables, decision trees, or reference data
71: 
72: **Naming**: `[topic]-reference.md`
73: - Example: `emoji-reference.md`, `validation-reference.md`
74: 
75: **Structure**:
76: - Tables or lists for quick lookup
77: - Decision matrices
78: - Classification systems
79: - Standards and conventions
80: 
81: **Use cases**:
82: - Emoji selection guides
83: - File type classifications
84: - Validation rule sets
85: - Naming conventions
86: 
87: ### Example Files
88: **Purpose**: Show working examples of skill outputs
89: 
90: **Naming**: `[topic]-examples.md`
91: - Example: `optimization-examples.md`, `skill-examples.md`
92: 
93: **Structure**:
94: - Before/after comparisons
95: - Annotated examples
96: - Multiple variations
97: - Anti-patterns to avoid
98: 
99: **Use cases**:
100: - Complete skill applications
101: - Common patterns
102: - Edge cases
103: - Quality standards
104: 
105: ### Guide Files
106: **Purpose**: Detailed how-to guides for complex processes
107: 
108: **Naming**: `[process]-guide.md`
109: - Example: `packaging-guide.md`, `distribution-guide.md`
110: 
111: **Structure**:
112: - Step-by-step instructions
113: - Troubleshooting sections
114: - Best practices
115: - Common pitfalls
116: 
117: **Use cases**:
118: - Multi-step processes
119: - Advanced techniques
120: - Workflow deep-dives
121: - Integration guides
122: 
123: ---
124: 
125: ## 3. DOCUMENT STRUCTURE
126: 
127: ### Title and Intro
128: 
129: **CRITICAL: The intro after the H1 title must be 1-2 SHORT sentences only.**
130: 
131: ```markdown
132: ---
133: title: [Title]
134: description: [One-line description - same as intro]
135: trigger_phrases:
136:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
137:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
138:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
139: importance_tier: normal
140: contextType: general
141: version: 1.0.0.0
142: ---
143: 
144: # [Title]
145: 
146: [1-2 SHORT sentences only. Brief hook/summary. NO subsections, NO headers here.]
147: 
148: \## 1. OVERVIEW
149: 
150: ### Purpose
151: 
152: [Why this asset exists]
153: 
154: ### Usage
155: 
156: [How to use this asset - copy instructions, customization notes]
157: 
158: ---
159: 
160: \## 2. [Content Section]
161: 
162: [The actual template/checklist/snippet content]
163: 
164: ---
165: 
166: ## N. Related Resources (optional, if present must be last)
167: 
168: [Links to related files]
169: 
170: ```
171: 
172: Every asset file carries this full 5-field frontmatter block: the Skill Advisor harvests it as routing signal (3-8 lowercase multi-word `trigger_phrases` drawn from the doc's content, `importance_tier` defaults to `normal`, and `contextType` is one of `planning|research|implementation|general`). See [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md) for field rules.
173: 
174: > **WARNING: DO NOT duplicate content between intro and OVERVIEW section.**
175: > The intro is a hook. OVERVIEW provides the details.
176: 
177: #### GOOD Intro Structure
178: 
179: ```markdown
180: # Git Commit Templates
181: 
182: Copy the template that matches the change, fill the fields, and commit.
183: 
184: \## 1. OVERVIEW
185: 
186: ### Purpose
187: 
188: Uniform messages let a reader scan history by intent instead of by author.
189: 
190: ### Usage
191: 
192: Copy the appropriate template based on commit type...
193: 
194: ---
195: 
196: \## 2. COMMIT TEMPLATES
197: ...
198: ```
199: 
200: #### BAD Intro Structure (too long, has subsections)
201: 
202: ```markdown
203: # Git Commit Templates
204: 
205: Copy-paste templates for creating well-structured commit messages.
206: 
207: ### Core Principle    ← WRONG: No headers in intro!
208: Atomic commits with clear intent = maintainable history.
209: 
210: ### When to Use       ← WRONG: This belongs in OVERVIEW section!
211: - Creating new features
212: - Fixing bugs
213: 
214: ---
215: ```
216: 
217: ### Intro vs OVERVIEW Content Placement
218: 
219: | Content Type          | Intro (after H1) | OVERVIEW Section       |
220: | --------------------- | ---------------- | ---------------------- |
221: | 1-2 sentence summary  | ✅ YES            | ❌ NO (don't repeat)    |
222: | Core Principle        | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |
223: | When to Use           | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Purpose)     |
224: | How to copy/customize | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Usage)       |
225: | Prerequisites         | ❌ NO             | ✅ YES (in Usage)       |
226: | Any H2/H3 subsections | ❌ NEVER          | ✅ YES                  |
227: 
228: ---
229: 
230: ## 4. STANDARD ASSET STRUCTURE
231: 
232: **Template**:
233: 
234: ````markdown
235: ---
236: title: Asset Title - Descriptive Subtitle
237: description: One-line description of what this asset provides
238: trigger_phrases:
239:   - "[distinctive phrase one]"
240:   - "[distinctive phrase two]"
241:   - "[distinctive phrase three]"
242: importance_tier: normal
243: contextType: general
244: version: 1.0.0.0
245: ---
246: 
247: # Asset Title - Descriptive Subtitle
248: 
249: Brief introduction (1-2 sentences) explaining what this asset provides and when to use it.
250: 
251: \## 1. OVERVIEW
252: 
253: ### Purpose
254: 
255: [Why this asset exists, what problem it solves]
256: 
257: ### Usage
258: 
259: [How to use this asset - copy instructions, customization notes]
260: 
261: ---
262: 
263: \## 2. SECTION NAME
264: 
265: **Key Points**:
266: - Point 1
267: - Point 2
268: - Point 3
269: 
270: **Template**:
271: ```[language]
272: # Template content here
273: # With explanatory comments
274: ```
275: 
276: **Field Guidelines**:
277: 
278: **`field_name`**:
279: - Description of field
280: - Format requirements
281: - Example: `value-example`
282: 
283: **Complete Example**:
284: ```[language]
285: # Complete working example
286: # Ready to copy and adapt
287: ```
288: 
289: ---
290: 
291: \## 3. SECTION NAME
292: 
293: [Continue pattern...]
294: 
295: ---
296: 
297: ## N. RELATED RESOURCES
298: 
299: [Links to related files - MUST be last section if present]
300: 
301: ````
302: 
303: ---
304: 
305: ## 5. LOGIC REPRESENTATION PATTERNS
306: 
307: **Purpose**: Guidelines for representing logic, workflows, and decision trees in asset files using structured formats instead of prose.
308: 
309: **Why Structured Logic?**
310: - **Clarity**: Executable-style logic is easier to understand than prose
311: - **AI-Friendly**: LLMs parse structured logic better than narrative descriptions
312: - **Maintainability**: Changes to logic are more visible in structured formats
313: - **Consistency**: Same patterns across all asset files
314: 
315: ### When to Use Each Format
316: 
317: **Use Python Pseudo-Code When:**
318: - Complex branching logic (multiple IF/ELIF/ELSE conditions)
319: - Function/method definitions with clear inputs/outputs
320: - State management or algorithmic processes
321: - Validation or transformation logic
322: - Examples: Mode detection, validation pipelines, decision functions
323: 
324: **Use YAML Structures When:**
325: - Configuration data (settings, options, parameters)
326: - Pipeline definitions (multi-step workflows with clear phases)
327: - Hierarchical workflows (nested processes)
328: - Metadata structures (categorization, tagging)
329: - Examples: Workflow definitions, configuration templates, feature matrices
330: 
331: **Use Markdown Decision Trees When:**
332: - Simple branching logic (2-5 branches)
333: - Visual flow representation (user-facing paths)
334: - Classification systems (type determination)
335: - Quick decision guides
336: - Examples: Document type selection, frontmatter requirements
337: 
338: **Keep Markdown Prose When:**
339: - Explanatory text and conceptual overviews
340: - Narrative examples with context
341: - Best practices guidance
342: - Introductions and summaries
343: 
344: ---
345: 
346: ## 6. DECISION LOGIC EXAMPLES
347: 
348: **Purpose**: Demonstrate how to convert markdown prose into structured decision logic.
349: 
350: ### Python Pseudo-Code: Mode Detection
351: 
352: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
353: ```markdown
354: Check user input for mode indicators:
355: - If "$quick" is present, use quick mode with auto-scaling depth
356: - If "$ticket" is present, use ticket mode with depth 10
357: - Otherwise, use interactive mode with depth 10
358: ```
359: 
360: **After (Python Pseudo-Code)**:
361: ```python
362: def detect_mode(request):
363:     """Detect execution mode from user request markers"""
364: 
365:     if '$quick' in request:
366:         mode = 'quick'
367:         depth = 'auto_scale_1_to_5'
368:     elif '$ticket' in request:
369:         mode = 'ticket'
370:         depth = 'depth_10_rounds'
371:     else:
372:         # DEFAULT TO INTERACTIVE
373:         mode = 'interactive'
374:         depth = 'depth_10_rounds'
375: 
376:     return mode, depth
377: ```
378: 
379: ### Markdown Decision Tree: Frontmatter Requirements
380: 
381: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
382: ```markdown
383: Different document types have different frontmatter requirements:
384: - SKILL.md files must have frontmatter with name, description, allowed-tools, and version
385: - Command files must have frontmatter with description and argument-hint
386: - Skill reference/asset files must have the 5-field block
387: - Knowledge files outside skill folders should not have frontmatter
388: - Spec files typically don't have frontmatter
389: ```
390: 
391: **After (Markdown Decision Tree)**:
392: ```
393: Document type?
394: ├─> SKILL.md             → MUST have frontmatter (name, description, allowed-tools, version)
395: ├─> Command              → MUST have frontmatter (description, argument-hint, allowed-tools)
396: ├─> Skill Reference/Asset → MUST have the 5-field block (title, description,
397: │                           trigger_phrases, importance_tier, contextType)
398: ├─> Knowledge (outside skills) → MUST NOT have frontmatter (remove if present)
399: ├─> Spec                 → SHOULD NOT have frontmatter (suggest removal)
400: └─> README               → No specific requirement (usually none)
401: ```
402: 
403: ### Python Pseudo-Code: Validation Logic
404: 
405: **Before (Markdown Prose)**:
406: ```markdown
407: Validate the document structure:
408: 1. Check if required sections exist
409: 2. Verify section ordering is correct
410: 3. Ensure frontmatter is valid (if present)
411: ```
412: 
413: **After (Python Pseudo-Code)**:
414: ```python
415: def validate_document(doc, doc_type):
416:     """Validate document structure and content"""
417: 
418:     errors = []
419: 
420:     # Check required sections
421:     required_sections = get_required_sections(doc_type)
422:     for section in required_sections:
423:         if section not in doc.sections:

20: > Turn a question about data into a single HTML file that opens in a browser and answers it.

24: ## 1. AT A GLANCE
25: 
26: | Aspect | What you get |

36: ## 2. OVERVIEW
37: 
38: ### What It Does
39: 
40: You describe the comparison a reader needs to make. The catalog in `references/catalog.md` turns that comparison into one row, and the row names the file that draws it. You copy that file, swap its data block and apply one colour system. A validator then proves the corpus still renders.
41: 
42: When a request names a local v3 `DESIGN.md`, or passes `--default` for the carried `evilcharts`
43: reference in the style library, `scripts/apply-design-md.cjs` derives the chart role
44: palette, typeface stacks and corner ladder from its documented tables. The script reuses the
45: corpus gates, refuses to write on a failure, and places a hash-bearing provenance comment in both
46: theme blocks. Site extraction remains the job of `sk-design-md-generator`. This packet applies the
47: reference it receives.
48: 
49: The visual register is shared by the corpus: a 16px semibold title, a muted 14px description, a two-row footer, bare axes with 12px tabular ticks, a horizontal dashed grid, measured bar and line geometry, positioned HTML tooltip cards and keyed legend chips. Each template accepts `?scheme=light` or `?scheme=dark` and sets `data-scheme` before it paints, so a capture can pin a scheme the host machine does not have.
50: 
51: One form is one file, so there is no gallery page to lift a block out of. The packet holds no per-request logic. It holds a corpus and the rules for picking from it.
52: 
53: ### Why This Packet Exists
54: 
55: Charts written freehand are the ones that break. The axis labels overlap at the third data point, the legend wraps under a narrow viewport, the palette runs out of distinguishable colors at series six. None of that shows up in a check. It shows up when someone opens the file, and by then the chart has already been sent to somebody.
56: 
57: A form file that already renders has had those problems solved once. Copying it and swapping the data keeps the solution and changes only the part that should change. That is the whole method, and it is why this packet is organized around a corpus rather than around instructions for drawing.
58: 
59: ### Why It Matters
60: 
61: - **A chart that renders where it was built renders where it is read:** the output is one file with no install step and no build.
62: - **The palette decision is made once:** colour systems are named and applied whole, so no artifact invents its own.
63: - **Regressions are catchable:** a validator over the corpus turns "the charts still work" into something you can run.
64:

18: # sk-design-chart
19: 
20: > Turn a question about data into a single HTML file that opens in a browser and answers it.
21: 
22: ---
23: 
24: ## 1. AT A GLANCE
25: 
26: | Aspect | What you get |
27: |---|---|
28: | **Use it for** | A chart that plots values a reader compares |
29: | **Invoke with** | "create a chart", "plot the data", a named form such as "treemap" or a direct read of `SKILL.md` |
30: | **Works on** | A dataset and the comparison someone wants to make from it |
31: | **Produces** | One self-contained HTML file, built from a form file and one colour system |
32: | **Corpus** | Twenty-nine chart forms across six question families, plus three stock colour systems and provenance-gated design-md deliveries |
33: 
34: ---
35: 
36: ## 2. OVERVIEW
37: 
38: ### What It Does
39: 
40: You describe the comparison a reader needs to make. The catalog in `references/catalog.md` turns that comparison into one row, and the row names the file that draws it. You copy that file, swap its data block and apply one colour system. A validator then proves the corpus still renders.
41: 
42: When a request names a local v3 `DESIGN.md`, or passes `--default` for the carried `evilcharts`
43: reference in the style library, `scripts/apply-design-md.cjs` derives the chart role
44: palette, typeface stacks and corner ladder from its documented tables. The script reuses the
45: corpus gates, refuses to write on a failure, and places a hash-bearing provenance comment in both
46: theme blocks. Site extraction remains the job of `sk-design-md-generator`. This packet applies the
47: reference it receives.
48: 
49: The visual register is shared by the corpus: a 16px semibold title, a muted 14px description, a two-row footer, bare axes with 12px tabular ticks, a horizontal dashed grid, measured bar and line geometry, positioned HTML tooltip cards and keyed legend chips. Each template accepts `?scheme=light` or `?scheme=dark` and sets `data-scheme` before it paints, so a capture can pin a scheme the host machine does not have.
50: 
51: One form is one file, so there is no gallery page to lift a block out of. The packet holds no per-request logic. It holds a corpus and the rules for picking from it.
52: 
53: ### Why This Packet Exists
54: 
55: Charts written freehand are the ones that break. The axis labels overlap at the third data point, the legend wraps under a narrow viewport, the palette runs out of distinguishable colors at series six. None of that shows up in a check. It shows up when someone opens the file, and by then the chart has already been sent to somebody.
56: 
57: A form file that already renders has had those problems solved once. Copying it and swapping the data keeps the solution and changes only the part that should change. That is the whole method, and it is why this packet is organized around a corpus rather than around instructions for drawing.
58: 
59: ### Why It Matters
60: 
61: - **A chart that renders where it was built renders where it is read:** the output is one file with no install step and no build.
62: - **The palette decision is made once:** colour systems are named and applied whole, so no artifact invents its own.
63: - **Regressions are catchable:** a validator over the corpus turns "the charts still work" into something you can run.
64: 
65: ---
66: 
67: ## 3. CHART OR DIAGRAM
68: 
69: This packet and `sk-design-diagram` both answer "make me a bar chart", so the boundary is worth stating before the first request rather than after a misroute.
70: 
71: | The artifact carries | Packet |
72: |---|---|
73: | Values a reader compares, ranks or tracks over time | `sk-design-chart` |
74: | A structure a reader follows: a flow, an architecture, a sequence, a state machine | `sk-design-diagram` |
75: 
76: The test is what the reader does with it. Someone reading a chart is comparing quantities. Someone reading a diagram is tracing a path.
77: 
78: The hub router draws the same line by name. The bare type names `sk-design-diagram` documents stay with it, and this packet answers the form names that packet has no file for along with the data-qualified phrasings such as "bar chart of". `SKILL.md` section 1 lists both sides.
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: ## 4. LAYOUT
83: 
84: | Path | What it holds |
85: |---|---|
86: | [`README.md`](./README.md) | This file: the packet overview and navigation |
87: | [`SKILL.md`](./SKILL.md) | The runtime contract: when to use the packet, the workflow, the rules |
88: | [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md) | The machine router: intent model, resource domains and the format-resolution rule |
89: | [`references/`](./references/) | The catalog, the colour systems and the template contract |
90: | [`assets/templates/`](./assets/templates/) | One self-contained file per chart form, copied whole |
91: | [`assets/style-reference/`](./assets/style-reference/) | One directory per Style Reference, each carrying its own `DESIGN.md`, `palettes.json` and proof sheets. A reference is carried here rather than read from a sibling library, so nothing outside the packet can change it |
92: | [`assets/style-reference/evilcharts/`](./assets/style-reference/evilcharts/) | The default reference, whose palette supplies the three stock colour systems every stock form reads |
93: | [`scripts/`](./scripts/) | The corpus validator, shared gate arithmetic and the local `DESIGN.md` applicator |
94: | [`manual-testing-playbook/`](./manual-testing-playbook/) | Operator scenarios for the packet |
95: | [`changelog/`](./changelog/) | One file per release, named `v[version].md` |
96: | [`screenshots/`](./screenshots/) | One PNG per template and example, mirroring the source layout, so a form can be judged without opening a browser |
97: 
98: ---
99: 
100: ## 5. LICENSING
101: 
102: Every chart, palette and script in this packet is authored here. Nothing is copied in from an outside chart library.
103: 
104: That is a constraint rather than a preference. This repository is MIT and public, so anything it ships is handed onward to every downstream reader under an MIT grant. Content carried in from a source that did not give that grant would put a recipient in breach of a license they never saw. So the corpus is written rather than gathered, and an outside library is read for ideas and never for bytes.

14: # README Template and Selection Guide
15: 
16: Use this template for project, skill, feature and component READMEs. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) for source-folder READMEs that explain package topology, files, boundaries and data or control flow.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. README SELECTION
21: 
22: README files answer two questions: what is this, and how does someone use or navigate it?
23: 
24: | Type | Use When | Template |
25: |---|---|---|
26: | Project | The repository or package needs a public entry point | This file |
27: | Skill | A skill needs human-facing context beyond `SKILL.md` | This file |
28: | Feature | A user-facing feature needs setup, usage or behavior notes | This file |
29: | Component | A reusable module has an API, examples or configuration | This file, trimmed |
30: | Code Folder | A source directory needs developer orientation | [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) |
31: 
32: Create a README when someone can land in the folder and need orientation. Skip it when inline comments or a nearby parent README already explain the folder.
33: 
34: ```text
35: Is this a project, package, skill or feature root?
36: +-- Yes: write a general README.
37: `-- No: is this source-code orientation?
38:     +-- Yes: use readme_code_template.md.
39:     `-- No: write a focused README only if readers need setup, usage or navigation help.
40: ```
41: 
42: Keep READMEs current-state only. Do not cite spec packet numbers, phase IDs or migration history. Use feature names, file paths, commands and stable source links.
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 2. GENERAL STRUCTURE
47: 
48: Use only the sections that fit the audience. Project and skill READMEs often need most sections. Feature and component READMEs should stay shorter.
49: 
50: | Section | Include When | Content |
51: |---|---|---|
52: | Overview | Always | Purpose, audience, main value and prerequisites |
53: | Key Statistics | Useful facts help readers decide scope | Counts, version, supported modes, limits |
54: | How This Compares | Readers may confuse this with nearby tools | Short comparison table |
55: | Quick Start | Readers need to run or try something | Short setup, verification and first use |
56: | Features | Capabilities need explanation | Feature groups, behavior notes and examples |
57: | Requirements | Runtime, tool or service needs exist | Minimum versions, permissions and external services |
58: | Structure | Navigation matters | Directory tree and key files |
59: | Configuration | Settings exist | Config files, options, defaults and env vars |
60: | Usage Examples | Patterns are easier shown than described | Simple and advanced examples with expected results |
61: | Troubleshooting | Users can hit known issues | What they see, cause and fix |
62: | FAQ | Repeated questions exist | Short answers only |
63: | Related Resources | Always when links exist | Grouped skills, documents, commands or external references |
64: 
65: Code-folder READMEs are different. Do not force Quick Start, Features, FAQ or Troubleshooting unless the directory has runnable commands or known reader problems. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md).
66: 
67: ---
68: 
69: ## 3. SKILL AND PROJECT PROFILE
70: 
71: Use this profile for OpenCode skills, package roots and project-level READMEs that need more than a bare overview.
72: 
73: | Profile Block | Good For | Keep It Short By |
74: |---|---|---|
75: | `trigger_phrases` | Search, memory and skill routing | 3-8 concrete phrases |
76: | Key Statistics | Skill counts, tool counts, version facts | Use one compact table |
77: | How This Compares | Neighboring skills or tools | Compare only reader-relevant differences |
78: | Key Features | Current capability inventory | Group related features |
79: | Requirements | Tooling and runtime needs | Separate required from optional |
80: | Related Skills | Skill graph navigation | Group by relationship type |
81: | Related Documents | Operator or developer references | Link stable docs, not packet history |
82: | FAQ | Repeated questions | 3-6 high-value Q&A pairs |
83: 
84: Sections use plain numbered H2 headings. Do not add `<!-- ANCHOR -->` comments or a Table of Contents.
85: 
86: ```markdown
87: ## 1. OVERVIEW
88: 
89: [Section content]
90: 
91: ```
92: 
93: ---
94: 
95: ## 4. WRITING RULES
96: 
97: Write for scanning first.
98: 
99: - Lead with what the thing does.
100: - Put the fastest useful path before detailed reference.
101: - Use tables for options, file lists and comparisons.
102: - Give every inventory item a description. When an item needs more than one line, switch to the itemized pattern below instead of widening the table.
103: - Use fenced code blocks with language tags.
104: - Test commands before documenting them.
105: - Show expected output for verification commands.
106: - Use relative links for local docs.
107: - Remove unused sections instead of leaving placeholders.
108: 
109: The itemized pattern for inventories where each item needs more than one line:
110: 
111: ```markdown
112: **`spec.md`**
113: - What the feature is and why it exists.
114: - Required at every level.
115: ```
116: 
117: Group related items under an unnumbered `#####` heading when the inventory has natural groups, for example by how each item is triggered.
118: 
119: Voice by README type:
120: 
121: | Type | Voice |
122: |---|---|
123: | Project, Skill, Feature | Plain explanation first, reference detail later |
124: | Component | Technical and concise |
125: | Code Folder | Technical and concise, via `readme-code-template.md` |
126: 
127: Human Voice Rules apply to all README content:
128: 
129: - No em dashes. Use commas, periods or colons.
130: - No semicolons. Split the sentence or use "and".
131: - No Oxford comma in inline lists.
132: - No setup phrases.
133: - No banned words from the HVR reference.
134: - Prefer active voice and direct verbs.
135: 
136: Full reference: [`hvr-rules.md`](../../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md).
137:

141:

145: ---
146: title: "[DOCUMENT_TITLE]"

24: | Type | Use When | Template |
25: |---|---|---|
26: | Project | The repository or package needs a public entry point | This file |
27: | Skill | A skill needs human-facing context beyond `SKILL.md` | This file |
28: | Feature | A user-facing feature needs setup, usage or behavior notes | This file |
29: | Component | A reusable module has an API, examples or configuration | This file, trimmed |
30: | Code Folder | A source directory needs developer orientation | [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) |
31: 
32: Create a README when someone can land in the folder and need orientation. Skip it when inline comments or a nearby parent README already explain the folder.
33: 
34: ```text
35: Is this a project, package, skill or feature root?
36: +-- Yes: write a general README.
37: `-- No: is this source-code orientation?
38:     +-- Yes: use readme_code_template.md.
39:     `-- No: write a focused README only if readers need setup, usage or navigation help.
40: ```
41: 
42: Keep READMEs current-state only. Do not cite spec packet numbers, phase IDs or migration history. Use feature names, file paths, commands and stable source links.
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 2. GENERAL STRUCTURE
47: 
48: Use only the sections that fit the audience. Project and skill READMEs often need most sections. Feature and component READMEs should stay shorter.
49: 
50: | Section | Include When | Content |
51: |---|---|---|
52: | Overview | Always | Purpose, audience, main value and prerequisites |
53: | Key Statistics | Useful facts help readers decide scope | Counts, version, supported modes, limits |
54: | How This Compares | Readers may confuse this with nearby tools | Short comparison table |
55: | Quick Start | Readers need to run or try something | Short setup, verification and first use |
56: | Features | Capabilities need explanation | Feature groups, behavior notes and examples |
57: | Requirements | Runtime, tool or service needs exist | Minimum versions, permissions and external services |
58: | Structure | Navigation matters | Directory tree and key files |
59: | Configuration | Settings exist | Config files, options, defaults and env vars |
60: | Usage Examples | Patterns are easier shown than described | Simple and advanced examples with expected results |
61: | Troubleshooting | Users can hit known issues | What they see, cause and fix |
62: | FAQ | Repeated questions exist | Short answers only |
63: | Related Resources | Always when links exist | Grouped skills, documents, commands or external references |
64: 
65: Code-folder READMEs are different. Do not force Quick Start, Features, FAQ or Troubleshooting unless the directory has runnable commands or known reader problems. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md).
66: 
67: ---
68: 
69: ## 3. SKILL AND PROJECT PROFILE
70: 
71: Use this profile for OpenCode skills, package roots and project-level READMEs that need more than a bare overview.
72: 
73: | Profile Block | Good For | Keep It Short By |
74: |---|---|---|
75: | `trigger_phrases` | Search, memory and skill routing | 3-8 concrete phrases |
76: | Key Statistics | Skill counts, tool counts, version facts | Use one compact table |
77: | How This Compares | Neighboring skills or tools | Compare only reader-relevant differences |
78: | Key Features | Current capability inventory | Group related features |
79: | Requirements | Tooling and runtime needs | Separate required from optional |
80: | Related Skills | Skill graph navigation | Group by relationship type |
81: | Related Documents | Operator or developer references | Link stable docs, not packet history |
82: | FAQ | Repeated questions | 3-6 high-value Q&A pairs |
83: 
84: Sections use plain numbered H2 headings. Do not add `<!-- ANCHOR -->` comments or a Table of Contents.
85: 
86: ```markdown
87: ## 1. OVERVIEW
88: 
89: [Section content]
90: 
91: ```
92: 
93: ---
94: 
95: ## 4. WRITING RULES
96: 
97: Write for scanning first.
98: 
99: - Lead with what the thing does.
100: - Put the fastest useful path before detailed reference.
101: - Use tables for options, file lists and comparisons.
102: - Give every inventory item a description. When an item needs more than one line, switch to the itemized pattern below instead of widening the table.
103: - Use fenced code blocks with language tags.
104: - Test commands before documenting them.
105: - Show expected output for verification commands.
106: - Use relative links for local docs.
107: - Remove unused sections instead of leaving placeholders.
108: 
109: The itemized pattern for inventories where each item needs more than one line:
110: 
111: ```markdown
112: **`spec.md`**
113: - What the feature is and why it exists.
114: - Required at every level.
115: ```
116: 
117: Group related items under an unnumbered `#####` heading when the inventory has natural groups, for example by how each item is triggered.
118: 
119: Voice by README type:
120: 
121: | Type | Voice |
122: |---|---|
123: | Project, Skill, Feature | Plain explanation first, reference detail later |
124: | Component | Technical and concise |
125: | Code Folder | Technical and concise, via `readme-code-template.md` |
126: 
127: Human Voice Rules apply to all README content:
128: 
129: - No em dashes. Use commas, periods or colons.
130: - No semicolons. Split the sentence or use "and".
131: - No Oxford comma in inline lists.
132: - No setup phrases.
133: - No banned words from the HVR reference.
134: - Prefer active voice and direct verbs.
135: 
136: Full reference: [`hvr-rules.md`](../../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md).

140: ## 5. FRONTMATTER
141: 
142: Frontmatter is optional for normal project READMEs and recommended for skill or system documentation that should be discoverable.
143:

146: title: "[DOCUMENT_TITLE]"
147: description: "[One-sentence description]"
148: trigger_phrases:

150:   - "[routing phrase]"
151: ---
152: ```
153: 
154: Use frontmatter when it improves routing, search or maintenance. Omit it for small human-only documents.

14: # Skill README Template
15: 
16: Use this template for `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/README.md`. It writes a skill README in the same narrative voice the repo root `README.md` and the changelogs use: a one-line human pitch, an at-a-glance table near the top, a value-first overview, then quick start, navigation and a verification close.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Purpose
23: 
24: Give a person a fast, honest orientation to a skill before they open `SKILL.md`. The README answers what outcome the skill delivers, when to reach for it, what it does not own and how to navigate its files. `SKILL.md` stays the runtime instruction surface. The README is the front door a person reads.
25: 
26: ### Identity Guidance (Purpose First)
27: 
28: The identity of a skill is the outcome it delivers. State that outcome in one plain sentence before naming tools.
29: Describe CLIs, commands, routing paths and reference files only after the outcome.
30: A README that opens with a tool name has not stated its identity.
31: 
32: The mcp-obsidian README states the outcome first: it makes AI use inside Obsidian effective.
33: It names the CLIs and MCP server later as delivery surfaces.
34: Repeat the outcome in the frontmatter description and the pitch.
35: The description supports a quick scan. The pitch opens the full README.
36: 
37: ### Usage
38: 
39: Copy the fillable scaffold in Section 6 into `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/README.md`, then replace every placeholder with current behavior taken from the skill's real files. Keep the numbered ALL-CAPS section headers, the house style and the validator both require them. Drop any section that does not earn its place and renumber the rest.
40: 
41: ### Template Focus
42: 
43: The README gives people a human entry point, current capabilities and a clear route to supporting files. This template provides:
44: 
45: - A one-line pitch in a blockquote right after the H1, stating the outcome before any tool name.
46: - An identity guidance block that puts the delivered outcome ahead of the tooling.
47: - A capability section pattern for a skill's headline strengths, modeled on the pilot's Plugin Knowledge Layer.
48: - A dedicated HVR enforcement section with the banned forms and the scripted checks.
49: - Versioning conventions and a validation checklist that matches the pilot's gates.
50: 
51: ---
52: 
53: ## 2. SECTION MODEL
54: 
55: A skill README uses numbered ALL-CAPS H2 sections with `---` dividers between them. The default order:
56: 
57: | # | Section | Purpose | Keep When |
58: |---|---------|---------|-----------|
59: | 1 | AT A GLANCE | Four-row table a reader scans in five seconds | Always |
60: | 2 | OVERVIEW | What the skill is and what the reader gets first, then the optional problem narrative | Always (required by the validator) |
61: | 3 | QUICK START | The fastest path to a first result | Skill has commands, scripts or a workflow |
62: | 4 | HOW IT WORKS | The main workflow in prose, with a small Mermaid diagram for multi-step flows | Skill has non-obvious behavior worth explaining |
63: | 5 | INTEGRATION & NAVIGATION | When to use it, plus how it hands off to sibling skills | Readers can confuse it with a neighbor |
64: | 6 | TROUBLESHOOTING | The failure modes operators actually hit | Predictable issues exist |
65: | 7 | FAQ | The two to five questions readers keep asking | High-value answers exist |
66: | 8 | VERIFICATION | How you know the skill works | Skill ships a playbook or validation command |
67: | 9 | RELATED DOCUMENTS | Stable links out, `SKILL.md` first | Always when links exist |
68: 
69: `OVERVIEW` is the one required section. Its normalized name must appear as a numbered header so the validator finds it. Every other section is optional. A small utility skill might run four sections (AT A GLANCE, OVERVIEW, QUICK START, RELATED DOCUMENTS). A large orchestrator might run all nine. Match the count to the skill. Never pad to hit a number.
70: 
71: Inside OVERVIEW, start with `### What It Does`. Say what the skill is and what the reader gets.
72: Add up to two optional subsections after it.
73: Use `### Why This Skill Exists` only to name a current reader problem.
74: Add the capability section below when it earns a table.
75: 
76: ### Capability Section Pattern
77: 
78: When a skill has a headline strength, add a named capability section after What It Does.
79: Use one or two short sentences to say why the strength matters.
80: Use an analogy only when it clarifies the mechanism.
81: Name the section after its domain and add one table row per capability.
82: State the file or data the skill can operate on.
83: Avoid marketing claims. The prose explains why the capability matters. The table states what it does.
84: 
85: ```markdown
86: ### The Plugin Knowledge Layer
87: 
88: | Plugin | What the skill knows how to operate |
89: |---|---|
90: | **Beancount Ledger** | append and patch balanced transactions in the structured `.beancount` ledger |
91: | **Obsidian Tables** | edit `columns`, `rows` and `views` inside `.table.md` JSON payloads |
92: ```
93: 
94: ---
95: 
96: ## 3. WRITING RULES
97: 
98: - Apply the [Prose Clarity Checklist](../../references/skill/creation-workflow.md#prose-clarity-checklist) to README prose.
99: - State the outcome before the tooling. The pitch and the identity guidance name what the reader gets. The tool names follow as the means.
100: - Open OVERVIEW with what the skill is and what the reader gets.
101: - Use `### Why This Skill Exists` only to explain a current reader problem.
102: - Add a short context hook after the blockquote only when it helps the reader. Keep AT A GLANCE as the first numbered section.
103: - Carry the explanation in prose. Reach for a table only when 4 or more parallel items need a lookup grid (skill relationships, CLI flags, a comparison).
104: - Use semantic emoji only (✅ ❌ ⚠️ 🔒 🚨) for rules and status markers. Decorative section emoji never: that register belongs to the repository front-page README, while a skill README keeps the technical formatting.
105: - A short, concrete analogy can carry an abstract mechanism better than adjectives (the repo root README uses "like a lab notebook for software"). Use one only where it clarifies, never as decoration.
106: - Put the AT A GLANCE table first. Four rows, one line each, no prose cells.
107: - Name the canonical command or entry point in OVERVIEW or QUICK START so a reader knows where to start.
108: - Link to real files under `references/`, `assets/`, `scripts/`, `feature-catalog/` or `manual-testing-playbook/`. Verify each path resolves.
109: - State the expected output for every command you show, so a reader can tell success from failure.
110: - Be honest about boundaries and trade-offs. If the skill does not own something, say which skill does.
111: - Keep `SKILL.md` as the runtime surface. The README explains why and how to navigate. It does not restate long reference files.
112: - Follow the Human Voice Rules. Section 4 lists the banned forms and the scripted checks. It links the full ruleset.
113: - Vary subsection counts rather than defaulting to three.
114: - Document current behavior. Keep spec history out of the README.
115: - Use stable paths and commands. Update the README, its version and its changelog entry when behavior changes.
116: 
117: ---
118: 
119: ## 4. HVR ENFORCEMENT
120: 
121: Every README this template produces must pass the Human Voice Rules. The full ruleset lives at [`hvr-rules.md`](../../../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md).
122: 
123: ### Banned Forms
124: 
125: The banned forms are: em dashes (U+2014), semicolons (U+003B), Oxford commas (a comma before the final and or or in a list), the hard-blocker words listed below and forced three-item groups.
126: 
127: ### Scripted Checks
128: 
129: Run the checks below from the skill root, with the README path as the argument. Each command must return zero matches. The punctuation checks use hex escapes on purpose: the commands stay clean of the characters they enforce.
130: 
131: ```bash
132: rg -n '\x{2014}' README.md
133: rg -n '\x{3B}' README.md
134: rg -n ',\s+(and|or)\b' README.md
135: rg -n '\b(delve|embark|realm|tapestry|illuminate|unveil|elucidate|abyss|revolutionise|game-changer|groundbreaking|cutting-edge|ever-evolving|shed light|dive deep|leverage|foster|nurture|resonate|empower|disrupt|curate|harness|elevate|robust|seamless|holistic|synergy|unpack|landscape|ecosystem|journey|paradigm|enlightening|esteemed|remarkable|skyrocket|skyrocketing|utilize|utilizing)\b' README.md
136: # Context-dependent words: landscape, ecosystem, journey, unlock, navigating
137: # Banned as metaphor, allowed in literal use. Judge each hit in context.
138: ```
139: 
140: The word check lists the hard blockers. A hit inside a code sample or a quoted command is exempt. A hit in prose is a violation. Context-dependent words from the full ruleset are banned as metaphor and allowed in literal use. Judge each hit in context.
141: 
142: Forced three-item groups are the fifth banned form. No exactly-three inline enumerations: use 2, 4 or 5 items. Tables and bullet lists are exempt. No exactly-three H3 subsections under every H2: vary the count.
143: 
144: ---
145: 
146: ## 5. VERSIONING CONVENTIONS
147: 
148: Every skill README carries a version in its frontmatter: `version: X.Y.Z.W`, the same 4-part scheme `SKILL.md` uses. Bump the README version on every release, whether the change touched the README text or the skill it documents. The README states the current state, so a behavior change is a README change even when the prose barely moves.
149: 
150: Every release gets a per-skill changelog entry at `changelog/<version>.md`. The entry follows the shared [changelog template](../../../sk-create-changelog/assets/changelog-template.md) and its message-release shape: NEW covers what arrived, CHANGED covers what moved, NOT CHANGED covers what stayed untouched.
151: 
152: `SKILL.md` and the README carry versions that move together. A skill release bumps both files. The changelog entry records the new version.
153: 
154: ---
155: 
156: ## 6. FILLABLE SCAFFOLD
157: 
158: Copy this into `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/README.md`, fill every placeholder from the skill's real files, then remove sections that do not fit and renumber.
159: 
160: ````markdown
161: ---

14: # Skill README Template
15: 
16: Use this template for `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/README.md`. It writes a skill README in the same narrative voice the repo root `README.md` and the changelogs use: a one-line human pitch, an at-a-glance table near the top, a value-first overview, then quick start, navigation and a verification close.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Purpose
23: 
24: Give a person a fast, honest orientation to a skill before they open `SKILL.md`. The README answers what outcome the skill delivers, when to reach for it, what it does not own and how to navigate its files. `SKILL.md` stays the runtime instruction surface. The README is the front door a person reads.
25: 
26: ### Identity Guidance (Purpose First)
27: 
28: The identity of a skill is the outcome it delivers. State that outcome in one plain sentence before naming tools.
29: Describe CLIs, commands, routing paths and reference files only after the outcome.
30: A README that opens with a tool name has not stated its identity.
31: 
32: The mcp-obsidian README states the outcome first: it makes AI use inside Obsidian effective.
33: It names the CLIs and MCP server later as delivery surfaces.
34: Repeat the outcome in the frontmatter description and the pitch.
35: The description supports a quick scan. The pitch opens the full README.
36: 
37: ### Usage
38: 
39: Copy the fillable scaffold in Section 6 into `.skilled/skills/[skill-name]/README.md`, then replace every placeholder with current behavior taken from the skill's real files. Keep the numbered ALL-CAPS section headers, the house style and the validator both require them. Drop any section that does not earn its place and renumber the rest.
40: 
41: ### Template Focus
42: 
43: The README gives people a human entry point, current capabilities and a clear route to supporting files. This template provides:
44: 
45: - A one-line pitch in a blockquote right after the H1, stating the outcome before any tool name.
46: - An identity guidance block that puts the delivered outcome ahead of the tooling.
47: - A capability section pattern for a skill's headline strengths, modeled on the pilot's Plugin Knowledge Layer.
48: - A dedicated HVR enforcement section with the banned forms and the scripted checks.
49: - Versioning conventions and a validation checklist that matches the pilot's gates.
50: 
51: ---
52: 
53: ## 2. SECTION MODEL
54: 
55: A skill README uses numbered ALL-CAPS H2 sections with `---` dividers between them. The default order:
56: 
57: | # | Section | Purpose | Keep When |
58: |---|---------|---------|-----------|
59: | 1 | AT A GLANCE | Four-row table a reader scans in five seconds | Always |
60: | 2 | OVERVIEW | What the skill is and what the reader gets first, then the optional problem narrative | Always (required by the validator) |
61: | 3 | QUICK START | The fastest path to a first result | Skill has commands, scripts or a workflow |
62: | 4 | HOW IT WORKS | The main workflow in prose, with a small Mermaid diagram for multi-step flows | Skill has non-obvious behavior worth explaining |
63: | 5 | INTEGRATION & NAVIGATION | When to use it, plus how it hands off to sibling skills | Readers can confuse it with a neighbor |
64: | 6 | TROUBLESHOOTING | The failure modes operators actually hit | Predictable issues exist |
65: | 7 | FAQ | The two to five questions readers keep asking | High-value answers exist |
66: | 8 | VERIFICATION | How you know the skill works | Skill ships a playbook or validation command |
67: | 9 | RELATED DOCUMENTS | Stable links out, `SKILL.md` first | Always when links exist |
68: 
69: `OVERVIEW` is the one required section. Its normalized name must appear as a numbered header so the validator finds it. Every other section is optional. A small utility skill might run four sections (AT A GLANCE, OVERVIEW, QUICK START, RELATED DOCUMENTS). A large orchestrator might run all nine. Match the count to the skill. Never pad to hit a number.
70: 
71: Inside OVERVIEW, start with `### What It Does`. Say what the skill is and what the reader gets.
72: Add up to two optional subsections after it.
73: Use `### Why This Skill Exists` only to name a current reader problem.
74: Add the capability section below when it earns a table.
75: 
76: ### Capability Section Pattern
77: 
78: When a skill has a headline strength, add a named capability section after What It Does.
79: Use one or two short sentences to say why the strength matters.
80: Use an analogy only when it clarifies the mechanism.
81: Name the section after its domain and add one table row per capability.
82: State the file or data the skill can operate on.
83: Avoid marketing claims. The prose explains why the capability matters. The table states what it does.
84: 
85: ```markdown
86: ### The Plugin Knowledge Layer
87: 
88: | Plugin | What the skill knows how to operate |
89: |---|---|
90: | **Beancount Ledger** | append and patch balanced transactions in the structured `.beancount` ledger |
91: | **Obsidian Tables** | edit `columns`, `rows` and `views` inside `.table.md` JSON payloads |
92: ```
93: 
94: ---
95: 
96: ## 3. WRITING RULES
97: 
98: - Apply the [Prose Clarity Checklist](../../references/skill/creation-workflow.md#prose-clarity-checklist) to README prose.
99: - State the outcome before the tooling. The pitch and the identity guidance name what the reader gets. The tool names follow as the means.
100: - Open OVERVIEW with what the skill is and what the reader gets.
101: - Use `### Why This Skill Exists` only to explain a current reader problem.
102: - Add a short context hook after the blockquote only when it helps the reader. Keep AT A GLANCE as the first numbered section.
103: - Carry the explanation in prose. Reach for a table only when 4 or more parallel items need a lookup grid (skill relationships, CLI flags, a comparison).
104: - Use semantic emoji only (✅ ❌ ⚠️ 🔒 🚨) for rules and status markers. Decorative section emoji never: that register belongs to the repository front-page README, while a skill README keeps the technical formatting.
105: - A short, concrete analogy can carry an abstract mechanism better than adjectives (the repo root README uses "like a lab notebook for software"). Use one only where it clarifies, never as decoration.
106: - Put the AT A GLANCE table first. Four rows, one line each, no prose cells.
107: - Name the canonical command or entry point in OVERVIEW or QUICK START so a reader knows where to start.
108: - Link to real files under `references/`, `assets/`, `scripts/`, `feature-catalog/` or `manual-testing-playbook/`. Verify each path resolves.
109: - State the expected output for every command you show, so a reader can tell success from failure.
110: - Be honest about boundaries and trade-offs. If the skill does not own something, say which skill does.
111: - Keep `SKILL.md` as the runtime surface. The README explains why and how to navigate. It does not restate long reference files.
112: - Follow the Human Voice Rules. Section 4 lists the banned forms and the scripted checks. It links the full ruleset.
113: - Vary subsection counts rather than defaulting to three.
114: - Document current behavior. Keep spec history out of the README.
115: - Use stable paths and commands. Update the README, its version and its changelog entry when behavior changes.
116: 
117: ---
118: 
119: ## 4. HVR ENFORCEMENT
120: 
121: Every README this template produces must pass the Human Voice Rules. The full ruleset lives at [`hvr-rules.md`](../../../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md).
122: 
123: ### Banned Forms
124: 
125: The banned forms are: em dashes (U+2014), semicolons (U+003B), Oxford commas (a comma before the final and or or in a list), the hard-blocker words listed below and forced three-item groups.
126: 
127: ### Scripted Checks
128: 
129: Run the checks below from the skill root, with the README path as the argument. Each command must return zero matches. The punctuation checks use hex escapes on purpose: the commands stay clean of the characters they enforce.
130: 
131: ```bash
132: rg -n '\x{2014}' README.md
133: rg -n '\x{3B}' README.md
134: rg -n ',\s+(and|or)\b' README.md
135: rg -n '\b(delve|embark|realm|tapestry|illuminate|unveil|elucidate|abyss|revolutionise|game-changer|groundbreaking|cutting-edge|ever-evolving|shed light|dive deep|leverage|foster|nurture|resonate|empower|disrupt|curate|harness|elevate|robust|seamless|holistic|synergy|unpack|landscape|ecosystem|journey|paradigm|enlightening|esteemed|remarkable|skyrocket|skyrocketing|utilize|utilizing)\b' README.md
136: # Context-dependent words: landscape, ecosystem, journey, unlock, navigating
137: # Banned as metaphor, allowed in literal use. Judge each hit in context.
138: ```
139: 
140: The word check lists the hard blockers. A hit inside a code sample or a quoted command is exempt. A hit in prose is a violation. Context-dependent words from the full ruleset are banned as metaphor and allowed in literal use. Judge each hit in context.
141: 
142: Forced three-item groups are the fifth banned form. No exactly-three inline enumerations: use 2, 4 or 5 items. Tables and bullet lists are exempt. No exactly-three H3 subsections under every H2: vary the count.
143: 
144: ---
145: 
146: ## 5. VERSIONING CONVENTIONS
147: 
148: Every skill README carries a version in its frontmatter: `version: X.Y.Z.W`, the same 4-part scheme `SKILL.md` uses. Bump the README version on every release, whether the change touched the README text or the skill it documents. The README states the current state, so a behavior change is a README change even when the prose barely moves.
149: 
150: Every release gets a per-skill changelog entry at `changelog/<version>.md`. The entry follows the shared [changelog template](../../../sk-create-changelog/assets/changelog-template.md) and its message-release shape: NEW covers what arrived, CHANGED covers what moved, NOT CHANGED covers what stayed untouched.
151: 
152: `SKILL.md` and the README carry versions that move together. A skill release bumps both files. The changelog entry records the new version.
153:

10: # Create Chart
11: 
12: `sk-design-chart` is the chart-authoring workflow packet of the `sk-design` parent hub. It produces a standalone HTML chart from a corpus of chart forms that lives inside this packet.
13: 
14: ---
15: 
16: ## 1. WHEN TO USE
17: 
18: ### Activation Triggers
19: 
20: Use this packet when the request involves:
21: 
22: - Building a chart that plots data: a ranked comparison, a part-to-whole split, a time series, a distribution, a relationship or a matrix.
23: - Deciding which chart form answers the comparison a reader needs to make.
24: - Choosing or applying one of the packet's three stock colour systems, or a provenance-gated design-md delivery.
25: - Applying a local v3 `DESIGN.md` Style Reference to a chart delivery.
26: - Adding a chart form to the corpus, or checking that the corpus still renders.
27: 
28: Keyword triggers: `create a chart`, `plot the data`, `data visualization`, `treemap`, `waterfall chart`, `heatmap`, `box plot`, `histogram`, `chart catalog`, `chart colour system`, `standalone html chart`, `measured site's look`, `theme a chart`.
29: 
30: ### When NOT to Use
31: 
32: Use a sibling packet when:
33: 
34: - The artifact explains a structure rather than plotting values. A flow, an architecture, a sequence or a state machine is `sk-design-diagram` work.
35: - The request is about the prose around a chart rather than the chart. That is `sk-create-readme` or `sk-create-quality-control`.
36: - The request asks to extract interface design values from a site. Extraction belongs to `sk-design-md-generator`; applying an already extracted local `DESIGN.md` stays here.
37: 
38: The boundary against `sk-design-diagram` is the one that actually gets tested, because that packet already names bar, line, scatter and radar in its own selection guide. The split is what the artifact carries. A diagram carries a structure a reader follows. A chart carries values a reader compares.
39: 
40: The hub router splits the packets by name. `sk-design-diagram` documents these bare type names:
41: 
42: - `bar chart`
43: - `line chart`
44: - `scatter plot`
45: - `radar chart`
46: - `gantt chart`
47: - `org chart`
48: 
49: This packet answers form names that diagram has no file for, such as:
50: 
51: - `treemap`
52: - `waterfall chart`
53: - `heatmap`
54: - `box plot`
55: - `histogram`
56: 
57: It also answers these data-qualified phrasings:
58: 
59: - `bar chart of`
60: - `line chart of`
61: - `scatter plot of`
62: 
63: If you name a bare type and ask for a diagram, the request reaches both packets. The router asks you which one you mean instead of guessing.
64: 
65: `radar chart` is the one name where the split by name and the split by artifact disagree, and the
66: two documents used to answer it differently with nothing saying so. By name it goes to
67: `sk-design-diagram`, which has a radar file and a type reference for it. By artifact it is values a
68: reader compares, which is this side of the line, and `catalog.md` section 6 records why this corpus
69: draws no radar and what answers the same comparison instead: `parallel-axes`, one scale per axis
70: rather than every dimension normalised onto one radial scale. Both hold, in that order. The name
71: routes to the diagram packet; a reader who arrives here comparing entities across several measures
72: is handed `parallel-axes` rather than sent away. The disagreement is recorded rather than resolved,
73: because resolving it means moving a file between packets and that is a decision about the hub.
74: 
75: ### Packet Boundary
76: 
77: This packet may create and edit chart artifacts, its own corpus and its own validator. It does not own the `sk-design` hub identity, and it never carries its own `graph-metadata.json` or `description.json`.
78: 
79: ---
80: 
81: ## 2. SMART ROUTING
82: 
83: The `sk-design` hub resolves a chart request here through `mode-registry.json`: the request plots values, names a chart form, or asks to theme a chart.
84: Below that point the packet routes on the comparison a reader needs to make, and selects packet-local resources only.
85: `references/catalog.md` loads first, because it resolves that comparison to one row, and the row names the form file under `assets/templates/` to copy whole.
86: A request that names a `DESIGN.md`, a style reference or a measured site's look loads `references/design-md-theming.md` and runs `scripts/apply-design-md.cjs`.
87: Read [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md) before selecting skill-local resources; open only the matched files.
88: When nothing matches, report `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` and ask which packet the reader meant instead of guessing.
89: 
90: ---
91: 
92: ## 3. HOW IT WORKS
93: 
94: The workflow is template-first, and that is a constraint rather than a preference. A chart assembled from a form file renders the way that file already rendered. A chart written freehand does not, and the failure shows up in a browser rather than in a check.
95: 
96: When the request names a `DESIGN.md`, a style reference or a measured site's look, route the
97: application branch to `scripts/apply-design-md.cjs`. It reads the v3 headings documented by
98: `references/design-md-theming.md`, derives both grounds from local values, and writes themed
99: copies only after the corpus gates pass. A request that asks for themed charts without naming a
100: reference runs it with `--default`, the evilcharts reference carried at `assets/style-reference/evilcharts/`. If the request asks to create the Style Reference itself,
101: route that extraction to `sk-design-md-generator`; this packet owns application, not extraction.
102: 
103: 1. Read the request and name the comparison the reader needs to make.
104: 2. Open `references/catalog.md` and resolve that comparison to one row.
105: 3. Copy the file that row names. Do not rewrite its render code.
106: 4. Swap the data block for the reader's data.
107: 5. Apply one colour system from the default reference's palette. One per artifact.
108: 6. Keep the result a single self-contained file. It opens in a browser with no install step.
109: 7. Run the corpus check before reporting the result: `node scripts/check-corpus.cjs` over the packet, and `node scripts/check-corpus.cjs --extra <dir>` over a delivery written outside it. Both must print `RESULT: PASSED`.
110: 
111: ### What the corpus holds
112: 
113: Use one file for each form.
114: 
115: The corpus contains twenty-nine chart forms across six question families: comparison, composition, time, distribution, relationship and matrix. `references/catalog.md` is the index. The corpus check reads it in both directions:
116: 
117: - A row that names a missing file fails.
118: - A file with no catalog row also fails.
119: 
120: There are no gallery pages to lift a block out of, because a chart reaches a reader as a delivery and a gallery ships every other form's demo data alongside the requested one. If no row answers your question, report the gap instead of improvising a form.
121: 
122: The corpus shares a measured visual register for card anatomy, type scale, bare axes, bar and line geometry, positioned HTML tooltip cards and keyed legend chips. Each template accepts `?scheme=light` or `?scheme=dark` and sets `data-scheme` before it paints, because a capture on a dark machine has no other way to see the light rendering.
123: 
124: ---
125: 
126: ## 4. RULES
127: 
128: ### ✅ ALWAYS
129: 
130: - Copy a form file that already renders, and change only its data block.
131: - Apply exactly one colour system per artifact; a `design-md` delivery is accepted only with its provenance comment and both inline gate checks.
132: - Produce a single self-contained file that opens with no install step.
133: - Run the corpus check before reporting a result: `scripts/check-corpus.cjs` over the packet, `scripts/check-corpus.cjs --extra <dir>` over a delivery written outside it, and require `RESULT: PASSED` from both.
134: - Author every chart and every palette in this packet.
135: 
136: ### ❌ NEVER
137: 
138: - Never copy a template, a fragment or a snippet from an outside chart library into this packet. The corpus is authored here, and content under a license this repository cannot grant onward must not enter the tree.
139: - Never write a chart freehand when a form for its question exists.
140: - Never mix two colour systems in one artifact.
141: - Never act as a separate advisor identity and never carry packet-level identity metadata.
142: 
143: ### ⚠️ ESCALATE IF
144: 
145: - No row in `references/catalog.md` answers the comparison the reader needs.
146: - The request wants a structure rather than values, which puts it on the `sk-design-diagram` side of the boundary.
147: - The corpus validator fails on a form you did not change.
148: 
149: ---
150: 
151: ## 5. REFERENCES
152: 
153: - `README.md` - packet overview and navigation.
154: - `references/README.md` - the reference index, which routes to the catalog, the colour systems and the template contract.
155: - `../mode-registry.json` - authoritative packet registration.
156: - `../hub-router.json` - parent routing policy.
157: - `../ROUTER.md` - stage-two leaf selection.
158: 
159: ---
160: 
161: ## 6. SUCCESS CRITERIA
162: 
163: - The artifact is one self-contained file that opens in a browser.
164: - The file traces back to one named row in `references/catalog.md`.
165: - One colour system is applied throughout.
166: - A local `DESIGN.md` can produce a deterministic, provenance-bearing delivery without changing stock forms or palettes.
167: - The corpus check printed `RESULT: PASSED` over the packet, and `--extra <dir>` printed it over the delivered file.
168: 
169: ---
170: 
171: ## 7. INTEGRATION POINTS
172: 
173: - Input: chart requests routed from the `sk-design` hub.
174: - Output: a standalone HTML chart.
175: - Neighbour: `sk-design-diagram` owns structural visuals, and the two are separated by what the artifact carries rather than by which one was asked first.
176: 
177: ---
178: 
179: ## 8. RELATED RESOURCES
180: 
181: - [`README.md`](./README.md) - what this packet is and how to navigate it.
182: - [`references/README.md`](./references/README.md) - the reference index for the catalog, the colour systems and the template contract.
183: - [`scripts/README.md`](./scripts/README.md) - what the corpus validator checks.
184: - [`../sk-design-diagram/SKILL.md`](../sk-design-diagram/SKILL.md) - the structural-visual packet on the other side of this boundary.
185: - [`../SKILL.md`](../SKILL.md) - the hub that routes here.

13: # evilcharts — Style Reference
14: > Neutral paper, one saturated accent per series, nothing decorative behind the data
15: 
16: **Theme:** light
17: 
18: evilcharts is a chart component library built on shadcn's tokens. Its language is a near-white
19: canvas, near-black ink and a hairline grey rule, with all of the colour spent on the series
20: themselves: five saturated chart hues that appear nowhere else in the interface. Chrome is
21: deliberately colourless, so a figure's only saturated marks are the ones carrying data. Corners sit
22: at a single 8.4px radius with a four-step ladder derived from it, and every figure is set in a
23: grotesque with a monospace reserved for numerals and code. The dark theme re-chooses its five chart
24: hues rather than lightening the light ones, which is the decision worth borrowing.
25: 
26: ## Tokens — Colors
27: 
28: | Name | Value | Token | Role |
29: |------|-------|-------|------|
30: | Canvas | `#ffffff` | `--background` | Page and card ground — pure white, the flattest possible backdrop for saturated marks |
31: | Surface | `#f8f8f8` | `--surface` | Raised panel and sidebar ground, one step off the canvas |
32: | Wash | `#f5f5f5` | `--muted` | Muted and secondary fills, the quietest occupied surface |
33: | Highlight | `#f2f2f2` | `--code-highlight` | Emphasised row inside a code block or table |
34: | Chalk | `#e8e8e8` | `--sidebar-accent` | Selected navigation ground |
35: | Rule | `#e5e5e5` | `--border` | Hairline borders, dividers and input outlines |
36: | Path | `#dfdfdf` | `--path` | Gridlines and axis paths inside a figure — one step below the rule so structure gives way to data |
37: | Halo | `#a1a1a1` | `--ring` | Focus ring |
38: | Slate | `#747474` | `--code-number` | Line numbers and the quietest legible label |
39: | Ash | `#484848` | `--muted-foreground` | Secondary text, axis ticks and captions |
40: | Ink | `#0a0a0a` | `--foreground` | Primary text and the primary action fill — near-black, never pure |
41: | Graphite | `#0b0b0b` | `--primary` | Primary button ground, a shade off the text ink |
42: | Flame | `#f54900` | `--chart-1` | First series — the orange that opens every multi-series figure |
43: | Teal | `#009689` | `--chart-2` | Second series — the cool counterweight to Flame |
44: | Deep | `#104e64` | `--chart-3` | Third series — the darkest chart hue, reads at small sizes |
45: | Gold | `#ffb900` | `--chart-4` | Fourth series — bright amber, intended for fills rather than thin strokes |
46: | Amber | `#fe9a00` | `--chart-5` | Fifth series — between Flame and Gold |
47: | Alarm | `#e32d36` | `--destructive` | Destructive action and error state; not a series colour |
48: | Pitch | `#090909` | `--background (dark)` | Dark canvas — the ground the dark chart set is chosen against |
49: | Snow | `#fafafa` | `--foreground (dark)` | Primary text on the dark ground |
50: | Slab | `#171717` | `--card (dark)` | Card ground on the dark theme, one step off the canvas |
51: | Cobalt | `#1447e6` | `--chart-1 (dark)` | First series on the dark ground — the blue that opens a dark multi-series figure |
52: | Jade | `#00bc7d` | `--chart-2 (dark)` | Second series on the dark ground |
53: | Violet | `#ad46ff` | `--chart-4 (dark)` | Fourth series on the dark ground; the one hue that carries a slot on both |
54: | Rose | `#ff2056` | `--chart-5 (dark)` | Fifth series on the dark ground |
55: 
56: ## Tokens — Typography
57: 
58: ### Geist Sans — Primary typeface for headings, body, navigation and every figure label. A neutral grotesque chosen so nothing in the type competes with the series colour; weights stay at 400 and 500 and headlines carry no bold. · `--font-geist-sans`
59: - **Substitute:** Inter, system-ui, -apple-system, Segoe UI, Helvetica Neue, Arial
60: - **Weights:** 400, 500, 600
61: - **Sizes:** 12px, 13px, 14px, 16px, 20px, 24px, 32px
62: - **Line height:** 1.20–1.60
63: - **Letter spacing:** 0 at body, tightening to -0.02em above 24px
64: - **Role:** Primary typeface for headings, body, navigation and every figure label.
65: 
66: ### JetBrains Mono — Monospace for every number a reader compares: tooltip values, axis figures, table cells, code and metadata. Tabular figures are the reason it exists here, so a column of numbers aligns on the decimal. · `--font-jetbrains-mono`
67: - **Substitute:** ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, SF Mono, Menlo, Consolas, Liberation Mono
68: - **Weights:** 400, 500
69: - **Sizes:** 11px, 12px, 13px
70: - **Line height:** 1.40
71: - **OpenType features:** `"tnum"`
72: - **Role:** Monospace for numerals, code and metadata — the technical voice.
73: 
74: ### Inter — Secondary sans carried for documentation prose alongside the primary grotesque · `--font-inter`
75: - **Substitute:** system-ui, -apple-system, Segoe UI, Helvetica Neue, Arial
76: - **Weights:** 400, 500
77: - **Sizes:** 14px, 16px
78: - **Role:** Secondary sans for documentation prose.
79: 
80: ### Type Scale
81: 
82: | Step | Size | Line height | Use |
83: |------|------|-------------|-----|
84: | caption | 12px | 1.40 | Axis ticks, legend labels, captions |
85: | body | 14px | 1.50 | Body copy and table cells |
86: | lead | 16px | 1.50 | Card subtitles |
87: | title | 20px | 1.30 | Card headlines |
88: | display | 32px | 1.20 | Page headings |
89: 
90: ## Tokens — Spacing & Shapes
91: 
92: ### Spacing Scale
93: 
94: | Step | Value |
95: |------|-------|
96: | 1 | 4px |
97: | 2 | 8px |
98: | 3 | 12px |
99: | 4 | 16px |
100: | 6 | 24px |
101: | 8 | 32px |
102: 
103: ### Border Radius
104: 
105: | Element | Value |
106: |---------|-------|
107: | inputs | 4.4px |
108: | buttons | 6.4px |
109: | cards | 8.4px |
110: | tiles | 8.4px |
111: | modals | 12.4px |
112: 
113: ### Shadows
114: 
115: | Level | Value |
116: |-------|-------|
117: | flat | none — surfaces separate by a hairline border, not by elevation |
118: | raised | 0 1px 2px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.05) |
119: 
120: ### Layout
121: 
122: | Property | Value |
123: |----------|-------|
124: | Sidebar breakpoint | 940px |
125: | Figure ground | Flat; no pattern, texture or image behind a plot |
126: 
127: ## Dark Theme
128: 
129: The dark ground is `#090909` with `#fafafa` ink and `#a1a1a1` for secondary text. The five chart
130: hues are **re-chosen, not lightened**: Cobalt, Jade, Amber, Violet and Rose replace the light set
131: rather than deriving from it. Only Amber appears in both, and it moves from fifth position on paper
132: to third on ink. Both sets sit in the colour table above, because both are tokens this reference
133: ships. Measured against the two grounds at the 3:1 a mark needs, four clear on both — Flame, Teal,
134: Violet and Rose. Deep and Cobalt clear only on white, and Gold, Amber and Jade only on ink, so
135: neither set on its own offers four hue-separated candidates for both themes. That is the decision this
136: reference is worth reading for: a hue that carries a slot on a white ground cannot always reach the
137: lightness that slot needs on a dark one, so the set is re-picked per ground.
138: 
139: ## Do's and Don'ts
140: 
141: - **Do** spend colour only on the marks. Chrome here is grey by construction, and a figure whose
142:   axis, rule and labels are neutral leaves the series as the only saturated thing on the page.
143: - **Do** set every number in the monospace with tabular figures, so a column aligns.
144: - **Don't** put a pattern, texture or gradient wash behind a plot. The ground is flat.
145: - **Don't** read Gold or Amber as thin strokes on white. Measured against this reference's own
146:   canvas they reach 1.72:1 and 2.13:1, below the 3:1 a mark needs; they are fill colours here.

43: | Teal | `#009689` | `--chart-2` | Second series — the cool counterweight to Flame |
44: | Deep | `#104e64` | `--chart-3` | Third series — the darkest chart hue, reads at small sizes |
45: | Gold | `#ffb900` | `--chart-4` | Fourth series — bright amber, intended for fills rather than thin strokes |
46: | Amber | `#fe9a00` | `--chart-5` | Fifth series — between Flame and Gold |

49: | Snow | `#fafafa` | `--foreground (dark)` | Primary text on the dark ground |
50: | Slab | `#171717` | `--card (dark)` | Card ground on the dark theme, one step off the canvas |
51: | Cobalt | `#1447e6` | `--chart-1 (dark)` | First series on the dark ground — the blue that opens a dark multi-series figure |
52: | Jade | `#00bc7d` | `--chart-2 (dark)` | Second series on the dark ground |
53: | Violet | `#ad46ff` | `--chart-4 (dark)` | Fourth series on the dark ground; the one hue that carries a slot on both |
54: | Rose | `#ff2056` | `--chart-5 (dark)` | Fifth series on the dark ground |
55: 
56: ## Tokens — Typography
57: 
58: ### Geist Sans — Primary typeface for headings, body, navigation and every figure label. A neutral grotesque chosen so nothing in the type competes with the series colour; weights stay at 400 and 500 and headlines carry no bold. · `--font-geist-sans`
59: - **Substitute:** Inter, system-ui, -apple-system, Segoe UI, Helvetica Neue, Arial
60: - **Weights:** 400, 500, 600
61: - **Sizes:** 12px, 13px, 14px, 16px, 20px, 24px, 32px
62: - **Line height:** 1.20–1.60
63: - **Letter spacing:** 0 at body, tightening to -0.02em above 24px
64: - **Role:** Primary typeface for headings, body, navigation and every figure label.
65: 
66: ### JetBrains Mono — Monospace for every number a reader compares: tooltip values, axis figures, table cells, code and metadata. Tabular figures are the reason it exists here, so a column of numbers aligns on the decimal. · `--font-jetbrains-mono`
67: - **Substitute:** ui-monospace, SFMono-Regular, SF Mono, Menlo, Consolas, Liberation Mono
68: - **Weights:** 400, 500
69: - **Sizes:** 11px, 12px, 13px
70: - **Line height:** 1.40
71: - **OpenType features:** `"tnum"`
72: - **Role:** Monospace for numerals, code and metadata — the technical voice.
73: 
74: ### Inter — Secondary sans carried for documentation prose alongside the primary grotesque · `--font-inter`
75: - **Substitute:** system-ui, -apple-system, Segoe UI, Helvetica Neue, Arial
76: - **Weights:** 400, 500
77: - **Sizes:** 14px, 16px
78: - **Role:** Secondary sans for documentation prose.
79: 
80: ### Type Scale
81: 
82: | Step | Size | Line height | Use |
83: |------|------|-------------|-----|
84: | caption | 12px | 1.40 | Axis ticks, legend labels, captions |
85: | body | 14px | 1.50 | Body copy and table cells |
86: | lead | 16px | 1.50 | Card subtitles |
87: | title | 20px | 1.30 | Card headlines |
88: | display | 32px | 1.20 | Page headings |
89: 
90: ## Tokens — Spacing & Shapes
91: 
92: ### Spacing Scale
93: 
94: | Step | Value |
95: |------|-------|
96: | 1 | 4px |
97: | 2 | 8px |
98: | 3 | 12px |
99: | 4 | 16px |
100: | 6 | 24px |
101: | 8 | 32px |
102: 
103: ### Border Radius
104: 
105: | Element | Value |
106: |---------|-------|
107: | inputs | 4.4px |
108: | buttons | 6.4px |
109: | cards | 8.4px |
110: | tiles | 8.4px |
111: | modals | 12.4px |
112: 
113: ### Shadows
114: 
115: | Level | Value |
116: |-------|-------|
117: | flat | none — surfaces separate by a hairline border, not by elevation |
118: | raised | 0 1px 2px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.05) |
119: 
120: ### Layout
121: 
122: | Property | Value |
123: |----------|-------|
124: | Sidebar breakpoint | 940px |
125: | Figure ground | Flat; no pattern, texture or image behind a plot |
126: 
127: ## Dark Theme
128: 
129: The dark ground is `#090909` with `#fafafa` ink and `#a1a1a1` for secondary text. The five chart
130: hues are **re-chosen, not lightened**: Cobalt, Jade, Amber, Violet and Rose replace the light set
131: rather than deriving from it. Only Amber appears in both, and it moves from fifth position on paper
132: to third on ink. Both sets sit in the colour table above, because both are tokens this reference
133: ships. Measured against the two grounds at the 3:1 a mark needs, four clear on both — Flame, Teal,
134: Violet and Rose. Deep and Cobalt clear only on white, and Gold, Amber and Jade only on ink, so
135: neither set on its own offers four hue-separated candidates for both themes. That is the decision this
136: reference is worth reading for: a hue that carries a slot on a white ground cannot always reach the
137: lightness that slot needs on a dark one, so the set is re-picked per ground.
138: 
139: ## Do's and Don'ts
140: 
141: - **Do** spend colour only on the marks. Chrome here is grey by construction, and a figure whose
142:   axis, rule and labels are neutral leaves the series as the only saturated thing on the page.
143: - **Do** set every number in the monospace with tabular figures, so a column aligns.
144: - **Don't** put a pattern, texture or gradient wash behind a plot. The ground is flat.
145: - **Don't** read Gold or Amber as thin strokes on white. Measured against this reference's own
146:   canvas they reach 1.72:1 and 2.13:1, below the 3:1 a mark needs; they are fill colours here.
